candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Even a cogent cosmological argument would support an evil creator as much as a good God and therefore cannot establish Craig's God without further arguments.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the cosmological question to Stephen, whose ensuing first-person answer contrasts Craig's God with an evil God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This applies the evil-God symmetry challenge directly to Craig's cosmological argument and contests its contribution to the cumulative case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that the universe's beginning deductively entails a timeless, spaceless, powerful personal creator.

candidates.contextSummary: After Craig describes what follows from a cause of the universe, Law argues that those conclusions do not identify the creator's moral character and require supplementation.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Not knowing why the universe exists is insufficient because the cosmological conclusion follows deductively unless one rejects either the universe's beginning or its transcendent cause.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks whether Law's profession of ignorance is sufficient, and Craig answers in the first person while restating his deductive premises.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move defends the logical force of Craig's cosmological argument and rejects the characterization of it as an appeal to gaps in scientific knowledge.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's answer that he does not know why the universe exists and his refusal to engage first-cause reasoning.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes a philosophical deduction from a God-of-the-gaps inference and says scientific evidence supports, but does not constitute, the premise that the universe began.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Acknowledging ignorance about why the universe exists does not prevent rationally excluding some answers, including an evil God whose existence the observed world's goods strongly disconfirm.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator invites Stephen to respond, and the ensuing first-person remarks explicitly compare his ignorance with the rational rejection of an evil God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the epistemic principle underlying Law's evidential challenge: incomplete explanation is compatible with strong evidence against a specified divine hypothesis.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that merely saying one does not know is inadequate unless a premise of the cosmological argument is denied.

candidates.contextSummary: Law distinguishes inability to answer an ultimate explanatory question from inability to rule out proposed answers, then uses observed goods to illustrate the distinction with evil-God belief.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Theists do not infer God's existence from an inductive inventory of worldly goods, so Law's observational comparison does not mirror the actual basis of Christian theism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly disagrees with Stephen and invokes theistic philosophers and a publication associated with Law while defending how theists reason.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection challenges whether Law's evil-God comparison accurately tracks the inferential structure of Craig's cumulative theistic case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's claim that the observed character of the world gives a powerful evidential case against an evil God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig answers Law's appeal to observed goods by denying that Christian theists establish God's existence through a comparable inductive survey of the world's good features.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The observational argument is not meant to establish a good or evil deity but to rule out a deity with a specified moral character when the world's features conflict with that character.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker immediately corrects Craig's description of the argument and restates in first-person terms what the observational inference is intended to establish.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This clarification preserves the core evidential symmetry by distinguishing evidence against a divine hypothesis from a positive inference to its moral opposite.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's objection that theists have never inferred God's existence from an inductive survey of worldly goods.

candidates.contextSummary: Law explains that worldly observations can exclude a deity of a certain character without proving the existence of the opposite deity, illustrating this with goods that count against evil God.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Human cognitive limitations prevent reliable probability judgments that apparently gratuitous goods or evils lack morally sufficient purposes within an omniscient being's providential plan.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker refers back to a point previously made from Stephen Wykstra and develops Craig's characteristic skeptical-theist response concerning divine purposes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's principal rebuttal to Law's observational evidential inference and directly challenges the probability judgment needed by both problem-of-evil formulations.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's claim that observable love, laughter, and other goods allow rational exclusion of an evil God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that an omnipotent and omniscient being may pursue ends inaccessible to human observers, undermining inductive judgments from apparently gratuitous features of the world.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The same appeal to inscrutable purposes can defend evil God, so skeptical mystery cannot defeat the observational case without an argument showing why humans cannot make the relevant judgment.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly applies Craig's skeptical strategy to evil-God belief and demands an argument rather than a bare assertion of unknowability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the direct symmetry counterreply to skeptical theism and argues that Craig's defense has an unacceptable consequence for the acknowledged rejection of evil God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's skeptical-theist claim that limited humans cannot judge whether apparent goods or evils serve unknown divine purposes.

candidates.contextSummary: Law argues that Craig's cognitive-limitation defense transfers unchanged to evil God, which people nevertheless reject, and insists that the alleged inability to judge requires independent support.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Historical consequences propagate beyond human epistemic reach, so people cannot know that a providential God lacks morally sufficient reasons for permitting a particular instance of suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: The answer recalls Craig's earlier citation of James Clerk Maxwell and articulates a providential ripple-effect account of morally sufficient reasons for suffering.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move provides Craig's requested argument for skeptical theism by identifying long-range causal consequences that constrain judgments about apparently gratuitous suffering.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's demand for an actual argument establishing why humans cannot judge divine reasons from observed goods and evils.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig grounds human uncertainty in the extended ripple effects of historical events, whose morally relevant outcomes may arise far outside an observer's lifetime or location.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Unexplained and apparently strong testimony arises predictably even for false extraordinary claims, so difficult-to-explain resurrection reports do not by themselves support the resurrection hypothesis.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Doctor Law to recap his fundamental objection, and the answer develops his earlier comparison with miracle, alien, and anomalous-object reports.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This attacks the resurrection component of Craig's cumulative case by denying that otherwise unexplained reports discriminate between the supernatural hypothesis and its falsity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's argument that historical evidence for Jesus's resurrection supports God's existence within his cumulative case.

candidates.contextSummary: Law uses a well-attested anomalous sighting later attributable to Venus to argue that some impressive cases will remain hard to explain regardless of whether extraordinary hypotheses are true.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Jesus's resurrection was unexpected within the disciples' Judaism and messianic expectations, distinguishing it from desired paranormal reports and adding explanatory warrant to the event.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly requests one brief response from Bill, and the answer contrasts the resurrection with reports generated by an appetite for paranormal phenomena.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This defends the resurrection evidence by contesting Law's expectation premise and identifying an allegedly distinctive feature of the disciples' reported belief.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's contention that hard-to-explain extraordinary reports are expected even when the extraordinary hypothesis is false.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that the disciples did not anticipate the resurrection because it conflicted with their inherited Jewish and messianic framework, reducing the force of Law's analogy.
